candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — safe medication administration, adverse effects, interactions and teaching
candidate.educational_objective: Apply the cited evidence to recognize the uniquely safest or most accurate nursing response in the clinical situation tested by V2-Q0109.

options.A: Separate grapefruit juice from felodipine by at least four hours because the interaction occurs only when both reach the intestine at the same time.
options.B: Replace grapefruit juice with orange juice only if the felodipine dose is increased because all citrus juices produce the same CYP3A4 inhibition at usual doses.
options.C: Grapefruit can markedly increase felodipine exposure and intensify blood-pressure effects; avoid it or clarify regular grapefruit use with the prescriber.
options.D: Limit grapefruit to a small serving with breakfast because clinically meaningful changes in felodipine exposure occur only with several large servings per day.

candidate.rationale: Felodipine is metabolized by CYP3A4. Current labeling reports that grapefruit juice can increase felodipine AUC and peak concentration by more than twofold, potentially increasing blood-pressure effects. The client should avoid or clarify grapefruit use rather than deliberately combining it with the drug.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Grapefruit juice increased felodipine AUC and Cmax by more than twofold; CYP3A4 inhibition can increase pharmacologic effects.
candidate.source_locator: Felodipine label — Drug Interactions/Food interaction: grapefruit juice increases felodipine exposure and pharmacologic effect
candidate.source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine; FDA-approved labeling)
candidate.stem: A client taking felodipine extended-release drinks grapefruit juice every morning. Which teaching is most appropriate?
